newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget deal revamps health care for poor.
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget deal revamps health care for poor.

text.p: U.S. governors won long-sought power to revamp state health programmes for the poor last week when Congress passed balanced budget legislation cutting Medicaid spending and ending key federal controls.

The budget measure, repealing a federal requirement that states pay "reasonable" nursing home rates and reducing aid to hospitals serving the indigent, could affect the quality and structure of health care offered the poor across the nation.
President Clinton is expected to sign the bill without delay.

Most of the attention during the budget debate focused on Medicare insurance for the elderly. Nearly as many Americans get health care through Medicaid, however, a state-federal programme covering about 37 million poor, elderly and disabled.
Medicaid pays more than half the nation's nursing home bills and insures a quarter of U.S. children.

"We're very pleased. The budget includes a number of the most important programme flexibilities the governors have been advocating for years," said Jennifer Baxendell of the National Governors' Association, which has long agitated for change.

The bill cuts Medicaid overall by about $15 billion over five years. It goes nowhere near as far a 1995 Republican plan to turn the programme into a grant to states. Lawmakers also rejected an administration proposal to cap spending.
Still the bill includes significant changes.
States are especially happy about repeal of a longtime law requiring them to provide "reasonable and adequate" Medicaid reimbursement for poor people in nursing homes and hospitals.

The so-called Boren amendment was originally designed to allow states to control Medicaid costs. In recent years it has given rise to a host of lawsuits as nursing homes have successfully challenged state payment schemes.
Nearly 70 percent of nursing home patients receive Medicaid, many middle class individuals who depleted their life savings on care that can cost more than $100 per day.

Patients' advocates worry states will now reduce payment, making it harder for Medicaid recipients to gain access to nursing homes. They also say industry might be tempted to raise rates to private patients.
"This needs to be watched pretty closely," said Lori Smetanka of the National Citizens' Coalition for Nursing Home Reform. "We don't want to see residents' health and safety jeopardised."
Analysts say while repeal provides an incentive for states to try to rein in nursing home costs, the industry has such a strong presence in legislatures it may avoid big changes.
The bill reduces federal matching payments for hospitals serving a large number of the poor by about $10 billion over five years.
Many states abused the so-called disproportionate share system over the years, coming up with creative financing schemes to draw down billions of dollars in federal financing.

Congressional aides said the new reductions should finally weed fraud out of the system. Some hospitals charge previous reform bills had taken care of most of the egregious abuses and the new round of cuts would pinch.

"Most of the Medicaid savings are going to be achieved by reducing payments to children's hospitals and other safety net institutions," said Peters Willson, vice president of the National Association of Children's Hospitals.

No state will get less than 3.5 percent below its fiscal 1995 Medicaid allotment. Lawmakers at the last minute added some money to help states like Texas and New York that have traditionally received high payments under the programme.

The bill also makes it easier for governors to move Medicaid recipients into managed care -- eliminating a requirement that at least part of a plan's caseload be private paying patients and easing federal regulations. It adds some new consumer protections to prevent abuse.

At the behest of governors, the state could pay lower Medicaid rates for individuals eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid. Some doctors refuse to treat Medicaid patients, complaining reimbursement is too low.

The bill also reduces payments to some community health centres. It includes some important new initiatives, including expansion of Medicaid to children as part of a companion child's health initiative providing $24 billion to states.
It guarantees Medicaid to tens of thousands of children who will lose disability aid under a new welfare law.
